edges.relationship: Co-authors of Structures of Indifference: An Indigenous Life and Death in a Canadian City (2018), on Brian Sinclair's death after 34 hours in a Winnipeg emergency room in 2008, read through the history of the city, the hospital and his life.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher page (University of Manitoba Press) re-read 2026-10-31 by researcher and reviewer: authors Mary Jane Logan McCallum (History, University of Winnipeg) and Adele Perry (History, University of Manitoba); September 2018, 192 pp.; Sinclair arrived in a downtown Winnipeg emergency room and 'Over a thirty-four- hour period, he was left untreated and unattended to'. Josh Manitowbi's review, Scientia Canadensis 43:1 (2021), pp. 117–118, as read by the researcher in the Érudit PDF: 'McCallum and Perry use a historical, place-based approach in their analysis of the systemic racism within Winnipeg's health-care system' (p. 117). He treats the argument as joint throughout and does not divide credit between the authors. The independent reviewer could not reopen Érudit (bot check) and confirmed only the review's Crossref metadata. The CHA's 2019 Indigenous History Book Prize citation also praises the book for 'writing collaboratively'. The book itself is unread. The edge records co-authorship only (precedent: Kealey ↔ Palmer as a comparison edge). It does not claim that either author's other work shares the book's argument.

edges.relationship: Collaborators in Shekon Neechie, the Indigenous-led history site founded in 2018 by seven Indigenous scholars: co-signatories of the board's 2021 open letter to the Canadian Historical Association and, with Susan M. Hill, co-authors of a 2024 account of why the founders built the site.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh readings 2026-10-31, re-checked by independent review the same day. (1) McCallum, Innes and Hill, The Conversation (Canada), 1 July 2024, read in full. Byline and Crossref record (DOI 10.64628/aam.pkfjpv6n4): McCallum, University of Winnipeg; Innes, McMaster; Hill, Toronto. Paragraphs are counted in the article body, skipping the five 'Read more' link boxes. The site was 'created by seven established Indigenous scholars on June 21, 2018' (¶1). 'We began creating the historian profiles due to frustration with a lack of public engagement in Indigenous historical scholarship' (¶18). Noticing few Indigenous historians presenting research at professional history conferences, the authors 'chose to create a publishing and public information alternative that is Indigenous-led and focused' (¶¶23–24). 'Shekon Neechie editorial board members also published an open letter responding to the denial of colonial violence' (¶30). (2) Open letter to the Council of the Canadian Historical Association and the Canadian Public, Shekon Neechie, 13 August 2021. This is a community-controlled site, so the letter is paraphrased, not quoted. It is signed by the seven board members as 'Shekon Neechie Board', McCallum second and Innes seventh. It supports the CHA's Canada Day Statement on the term genocide, answers the open letter signed by fifty-three historians, and names no historian. The 2024 essay is a co-authored public explanation, not a research article. The edge records collaboration (co-founding, co-signing, co-authoring), not a claim that their scholarship shares one argument. Also attested but not relied on: the site's 2020 podcast episode, hosted by Innes with McCallum as a guest (audio unheard).

edges.relationship: McCallum takes Philip Deloria's argument that understanding Indian modernity means investigating the frames non-Indians use to explain and contain Indian people, and names professional history as one of those frames, in 'Indigenous Labor and Indigenous History' (2009).
edges.evidence_note: Opening passage of the article (American Indian Quarterly 33:4, 2009, first page p. 523), read 2026-10-31 as the publisher's excerpt carried in the Semantic Scholar record for DOI 10.1353/aiq.2009.a362033; Project MUSE served a bot check. Re-checked by independent review. She writes that the article answered a Western History Association call for papers by Indigenous academics on 'working from home'. She wanted 'to make visible a division that separates Native people as history and Native people as historians', and to do so by historicizing 'the twentiethcentury English Canadian historical profession' [sic, as printed in the excerpt]. She continues: 'Philip Deloria argues that part of a project of understanding Indian modernity is to take as the subject of investigation the ideological and discursive frames non-Indians use to explain and contain Indian people. One of these frames is professional history.' The excerpt names neither the Deloria work nor his middle initial. He is identified as Philip J. Deloria, the historian of Indian modernity (Indians in Unexpected Places, 2004), from the subject of the sentence; that is an inference. The legal scholar Philip S. Deloria is a namesake. The rest of the article (pp. 524–544) is unread. This is a named use in her framing paragraph; no claim is made about how far the rest of the article depends on Deloria.
edges.map_label: Professional history as a containing frame, 2009

edges.relationship: Turns Indigenous history on the historical profession itself: historicizing twentieth-century English-Canadian professional history to show a division between Native people as history and Native people as historians (2009), and closing her 2014 book on the professional status and absence of Indigenous historians.
edges.evidence_note: (1) 2009 article, opening passage read as above (p. 523): the division 'that separates Native people as history and Native people as historians'; 'history' meant 'largely as the modern, paid labor of professional historians and the academic discipline of history'. (2) Carol Williams's review of the 2014 book, BC Studies 191 (2016), pp. 162–164, read in full 2026-10-31 and re-checked by independent review. Paragraphs are counted from 'Historian Patrick Wolfe…'. At ¶7, in her concluding chapter McCallum 'discusses labour disparities in Canadian university history departments, reflects on the professional status and glaring absence of Indigenous historians in academia, and proposes a critical revision of historiographical methods and pedagogy'. The publisher's contents list the conclusion as 'The Wages of Whiteness and the Indigenous Historian'. The conclusion itself is unread. The coordinator's draft left out an edge to this entry because she is already a representative person there. That roster row is not an edge, and this claim (a critique of the profession) differs from her existing archive and community-engaged edges.
edges.map_label: Native people as history and as historians, 2009–14

edges.relationship: Indigenous women's paid work, 1940–80, as labour history: domestic service, hairdressing under the 1957 placement programme, community health representatives and nurses, and the state schemes that directed their labour (2014).
edges.evidence_note: Two reviews re-read in full 2026-10-31 and re-checked by independent review. Harms, Manitoba History 80 (2016), paragraphs counted from 'Within the Canadian imaginary…'. ¶3: domestic service, and the link between the education offered to Aboriginal women and the labour they were offered. ¶4: hairdressing as a lens on the Indian Placement and Relocation Program from 1957, in which 'Indian Affairs attempted to control Aboriginal labour'. ¶5: community health representatives and the Registered Nurses of Canadian Indian Ancestry (1975). ¶7: the book is of interest to labour studies and to Aboriginal, women's and medical history. Williams, BC Studies 191 (2016), paragraphs counted from 'Historian Patrick Wolfe…'. ¶3: 'aboriginal women's lives inescapably involved in modern labour that was highly regulated by the Canadian nation-state'. ¶6: the 1957 Placement Program was 'the first organized national labour program'. ¶7: of interest to 'students of labour history'. The book is unread (publisher's contents only). Target: the general labour history entry. The reviewers say 'labour history' and 'labour studies', not Canadian working-class history.

edges.relationship: Places Indigenous women at the centre of a history of modern labour and state policy in Canada, and of their resistance through training and professional organizing (2014).
edges.evidence_note: Harms (2016), ¶2: 'Placing Aboriginal women at the center of the story', and the book's focus on how women 'adapted, resisted, and strategized within the parameters of modern Canada'. Williams (2016), paragraphs counted from 'Historian Patrick Wolfe…'. ¶3: 'aboriginal women's lives inescapably involved in modern labour'. ¶4: 'Yet women, as McCallum counters, were not passive', with training 'in feminine-specific occupations, including hairdressing' and the nurses' professional advocacy organizations. Both reviews were read in full 2026-10-31 and re-checked by independent review; the book is unread. The edge is bounded to the reviewers' accounts of the 2014 book.
edges.map_label: Indigenous women, work and the state, 2014

edges.relationship: Indigenous health history as a history of colonialism: a historiographical framing through starvation, experimentation, segregation and trauma (2017), and, with Adele Perry, a history of racism in Winnipeg's health-care system told through one man's death in an emergency room (2018).
edges.evidence_note: (1) CHR 98:1 (2017), author abstract only (existing source of the medical history entry): a historiographical framing of Indigenous health history through starvation, experimentation, segregation and trauma, not new clinical evidence. (2) University of Manitoba Press page for the 2018 book, re-read 2026-10-31 by researcher and reviewer. It asks what an Indigenous death in a Winnipeg emergency room reveals about 'the ongoing history of colonialism', and the publisher files the book under Medical History. (3) Canadian Historical Association, Indigenous History Book Prize 2019, jury citation (read by the reviewer 2026-10-31): the book 'serves as a corrective to the erasure of Sinclair and the denial of the violent roles played by racism and settler colonialism in Canada's so-called universal health care system'. (4) Manitowbi, Scientia Canadensis 43:1 (2021), pp. 117–118, as read by the researcher in the Érudit PDF. The authors 'examine the roots of racialized medicine in the history of Anishinaabe land and cultural dispossession, racial segregation, settler-colonialist racist beliefs, substandard education and health services' (p. 117). The inquest minimized 'stereotyping, false assumptions, and racism within the health care setting' (p. 117, quoting the book, 107). Its limitation is that it offers no recommendations for combating racism in health care (p. 118). The independent reviewer could not reopen Érudit (bot check) and confirmed only the review's Crossref metadata. If those quotations cannot be re-checked before release, the edge stands on (1)–(3). The 2018 book is co-authored with Adele Perry; the 2017 article is hers alone. Both books are unread.

edges.relationship: Structures of Indifference (with Adele Perry, 2018) places Brian Sinclair's death in a Winnipeg emergency room within the settler colonial history of Manitoba, and reads it as evidence of the racism and settler colonialism of Canadian health care.
edges.evidence_note: (1) CHA Indigenous History Book Prize 2019, jury citation (read by the reviewer 2026-10-31). The book 'situates the life and death of Brian Sinclair within the complicated settler colonial histories of the geographic area that came to be known as Manitoba', and corrects 'the denial of the violent roles played by racism and settler colonialism in Canada's so-called universal health care system'. (2) Publisher page, re-read 2026-10-31: the book asks 'what it reveals about the ongoing history of colonialism'. Sherene Razack's blurb calls it a framing of Sinclair's death as 'a racism that is the basis of Canadian settler colonialism'. G. Bruyere's CHOICE blurb says the authors analyse how the inquest's legal processes 'obscure the violence of contemporary settler colonialism'. (3) Manitowbi (2021), p. 118, as read by the researcher in the Érudit PDF: the book's 'primary strength' is its account of Sinclair's life and death and 'the history and persistence of settler colonialism in the Canadian health-care system'. He also quotes a sentence of the authors' own (book p. 102). The reviewer could not reopen Érudit, so the authors' wording is not used in graph text. All of these are readers' framings; the book is unread. No claim is made that the authors adopt Wolfe's theory. The settler colonialism entry's caution that McCallum (2014) wrote 'beside' the paradigm still stands for the 2014 book; this edge rests on the 2018 book.
edges.map_label: Settler colonialism in Canadian health care, 2018

edges.relationship: Interviewing Saskatchewan Aboriginal Second World War veterans, Innes argued that a Native Studies approach rejects the hierarchical researcher–researched relationship and that conventional oral history methods are problematic in an Aboriginal context (1999–2000).
edges.evidence_note: Gladue Rights Research Database record (University of Saskatchewan, with Legal Aid Saskatchewan and the Law Society of Saskatchewan): the excerpt of p. 64, and the attached PDF of the article (pp. 63–88), read 2026-10-31 for its method passages. On p. 64, Native Studies 'challenges the conventional historical methodologies' and 'also challenges the conventional oral historical methodology'. It 'rejects the hierarchical researcher-researched relationship', and the researcher must be 'flexible to accommodate the interviewee's mode of communication'. Excerpts from three veterans' interviews are used to show that 'conventional oral historical methodologies are problematic in an Aboriginal context'. On p. 65, Vansina's widely accepted definition of oral tradition 'tends to promote a static view of orally transmitted narratives'. On p. 69, following Turner's standardized questions and Henige's insistence that the historian control the interview 'would prove problematic' in Native Studies research. Nothing from the interviews is used. The edge targets the field because the article's critique is of conventional oral-history method as practised by several scholars (Vansina, Henige, Turner), none of whom is an atlas endpoint. It is distinct from Wheeler's existing critique of outside definitions of oral history (edge_2179).
edges.map_label: Native Studies against conventional oral history methods, 1999–2000

edges.relationship: Collaborators who launched Shekon Neechie, an Indigenous-controlled history site, from the University of Saskatchewan in June 2018, with Innes as its originator, and co-signatories of the board's 2021 open letter supporting the Canadian Historical Association's statement on genocide.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh readings 2026-10-31. University of Saskatchewan News (Shannon Boklaschuk, 28 June 2018), read in full: 'Two University of Saskatchewan professors have collaborated with other Canadian academics' (¶1); Innes and Wheeler 'serve on Shekon Neechie's managing board' with Indigenous scholars from other universities (¶3); Innes on how 'the idea for the website was born' and on recruiting senior Indigenous historians to 'open the pathways for others to come' (¶¶4–6); Wheeler, 'a professor of Indigenous studies since 1988', on why 'creating our own space was really important for us' (¶10). The 2021 open letter (Shekon Neechie, 13 August 2021; community-controlled, paraphrased) is signed by the seven board members including Wheeler and Innes. Also attested, not relied on: Innes hosted the 2020 podcast episode with Wheeler as a guest (audio unheard). The edge records an institutional collaboration and a co-signed public statement, not a shared research argument; no co-written research article by the two was found.

edges.relationship: Argued that Indigenous researchers, who had not yet joined the insider/outsider debate over research in home communities, should take it up (2009). Argued that Cowessess First Nation's kinship-based membership practices undermine legal and scholarly definitions of 'Indian' (2013).
edges.evidence_note: (1) 'Wait a Second. Who Are You Anyways?', American Indian Quarterly 33:4 (2009): 440–461. The opening passage (first page) was read 2026-10-31 as the publisher's excerpt in the Semantic Scholar record (Project MUSE blocked) and re-checked by independent review. Critics claim insiders' closeness 'clouds their views'. Insiders counter with 'a contextual understanding of the community that outsiders do not possess'. 'Indigenous researchers have not joined the insider/outsider debate to any significant extent', and they 'have much to gain from the experiences of other insider researchers'. The rest of the article is unread. (2) Elder Brother and the Law of the People (University of Manitoba Press, November 2013), publisher page re-read 2026-10-31. In the publisher's account, Innes shows how kinship practices at Cowessess 'act to undermine legal and scholarly definitions of "Indian"'. The book is unread, and the claim is bounded to the publisher's account of its argument. Nothing of the stories or community practices the book discusses is given here. Not a duplicate: his existing edges go to Indigenous–newcomer relations (two critiques) and to community-engaged research (the TLE count of the dead). An edge from the 2009 article to community-engaged research would duplicate that endpoint and kind, so both works are joined here.
edges.map_label: Insider research; kinship against definitions of 'Indian', 2009–13

edges.relationship: In her 1999 dissertation Emma LaRocque recommends Miller's Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989) as an overview of treaties, the Indian Act, reserves, residential schools and Métis land loss. She also cites 'Miller' with Frideres, Ponting, Dickason and Green for the point that colonial forces acting on Native peoples in Canada were institutional rather than military.
edges.evidence_note: LaRocque, Native Writers Resisting Colonizing Practices in Canadian Historiography and Literature (PhD, University of Manitoba, 1999), University of Manitoba repository PDF, read 2026-10-31 at the passages concerned and re-checked by independent review (text layer; OCR slips corrected). PDF p. 56, n. 15: 'For a good overview of treaties, the Indian Act, reserves, residential schools and Metis loss of lands see Frideres, Aboriginal Peoples in Canada; Miller, Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens; Dickason, Canada's First Nations.' PDF p. 133: the colonial forces 'have not been military, as a rule, but rather, have been institutional through economic, religious, educational legislative, and media systems (Frideres, Ponting, Miller, Dickason, Green)'. That parenthetical gives no title. Her bibliography lists both 'Miller, J.R. Skyscrapers hide the heavens' (1989) and Christine Miller and Patricia Chuchryk, eds., Women of the First Nations (1997). Reading the p. 133 'Miller' as J. R. Miller is an inference from its context and from n. 15. This is a recommended overview and a citation in argument, not an endorsement of Miller's whole interpretation. LaRocque elsewhere criticises settler 'cross-cultural' historians (her edges to Van Kirk, Brown and Trigger), and Miller is not among those she names there. No Miller text read.
edges.map_label: Cited by LaRocque as overview and authority, 1999

edges.relationship: Keith Wailoo (2020) notes that Rosenberg studied with Richard Hofstadter and reads the style of The Cholera Years (1962) as evoking Hofstadter's work.
edges.evidence_note: A named reader's claim, read. Keith Wailoo, ‘The Enduring Significance of The Cholera Years’, The Panorama (SHEAR), 22 September 2020, third body paragraph: ‘In style, the book evokes the work of Richard Hofstadter with whom Rosenberg studied.’ The first body paragraph places the book (1962; reissued 1987) as an early example of medicine's social-historical turn. Wailoo writes as an appreciative reader of a ‘classic’; this is a stylistic and pedagogical reading, not a demonstration of argued intellectual debt. Warwick Anderson's essay (University of Chicago Press journal, doi 10.1086/712234), which a search snippet reports as calling Rosenberg Hofstadter's student, returned 403 and is unread; the Mantovani interview (2016, read pp. 213–216) names Ackerknecht and Rosen, not Hofstadter, as formative, so the claim is limited to studentship and style. Rosenberg's dissertation and any acknowledgment in the 1962 book are unread. Reviewer 2026-10-31: Wailoo does not say 'doctoral student' or name Columbia; the AHA dissertations directory (repository harvest, record for 'The Cholera Years', Columbia, 1961) gives no adviser, so supervision by Hofstadter is not claimed.

edges.relationship: In ‘Disease in History: Frames and Framers’ (1989) Rosenberg calls the social construction of illness ‘in an important sense … no more than a tautology’, avoids the term because it overemphasizes functionalist ends and arbitrariness, and argues that the main trends in the history of disease, social-control readings among them, lose sight of the process of disease definition itself and its consequences.
edges.evidence_note: His own text, read in the Milbank Memorial Fund's open archive copy of The Milbank Quarterly 67, Suppl. 1 (1989), pp. 1–15. p. 2: ‘Much has been written during the past two decades about the social construction of illness. But in an important sense this is no more than a tautology’; the position ‘still serves to remind us’ that medical thought is rarely free of social constraint. p. 3: ‘I have, in fact, avoided the term social construction. I felt it has tended to overemphasize functionalist ends and the degree of arbitrariness’ and focused on ‘a handful of socially resonant diagnoses’; he uses ‘the less programmatically charged metaphor “frame”’. pp. 3–4 list five trends in disease history (social history; public health and the demographic transition; an ecological ‘new materialism’; demography; and, ‘perhaps most widely influential’, disease definitions as ‘a tool of social control’, citing Wright and Treacher 1982 and Figlio 1978, in which physicians are construed as agents of ‘a broader hegemonic enterprise’); p. 4: ‘What is often lost sight of in each of these emphases—and in the aggregate in all—is the process of disease definition itself’ and its consequences. The ‘lost sight of’ sentence applies to all five trends, not to social-control readings alone. A critique within a field he also built (his contribution edge edge_2946 remains): it qualifies the constructionist and social-control strands of medical history, it does not reject social history of medicine, which he calls necessarily ‘social’ (p. 3). The essay was reprinted as the introduction to Framing Disease (with Janet Golden, 1992) and in Explaining Epidemics (1992); those reprints were not collated. Named targets (Wright, Treacher, Figlio) are not atlas endpoints.

edges.relationship: ‘Fear and Anxiety: Writing about Emotion in Modern History’ (2003) appraises emotionology, social constructivism, narrativization and psycho-historical methods and, using fear as its example, argues that insufficient attention has been paid to physiology and to how emotions mediate between the individual and the social; it characterizes a new history of the emotions as ‘aesthesiology’ (article abstract).
edges.evidence_note: Abstract only, read on the publisher page (History Workshop Journal 55, 2003, 111–133, doi 10.1093/hwj/55.1.111) and in the Birkbeck eprint record (no full text deposited). The abstract says the article ‘examines and appraises some approaches to the analysis of emotional experience in history’ (emotionology, social constructivism, narrativization, psychohistory), finds that ‘insufficient attention has been paid to physiology’ and to emotions' mediating role, argues via fear and anxiety that emotions are ‘fundamentally concerned with power relations’, and defines ‘aesthesiology’ as ‘the emotional reaction of the self to stimuli in lived experience’. The body is unread (paywall), so the claim is bounded to the abstract: which authors she criticizes, and how, is not established. A critique within the field she contributes to; edge_2841 (contribution) remains.

edges.relationship: Phantoms of Remembrance (1994) studies how eleventh-century people (women praying for their dead, monks keeping and reshaping archives, scribes choosing which royal pasts to celebrate or forget) preserved the past or formulated the past they preferred to imagine.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher description read (Princeton University Press, book page; copyright 1994, paperback 1996): the book ‘makes important new inroads into the widely discussed topic of historical memory’, describes practices of remembrance in written and nonwritten forms, gives ‘women praying for their dead, monks creating and re-creating their archives’ and scribes deciding ‘which royal families of the past to applaud and which to forget’, and shows people ‘formulating the past that an individual or group prefers to imagine’. The page quotes Alexander Murray (TLS) on ‘three case-studies’ of ‘local patterns of memory’. The book is unread; this is a publisher's account. Date confirmed by the CV entry already on the atlas (tc234_geary_cv). Replaces the memory edge held in revision 1.234 because the IAS page refused access; no claim is made about which memory theorists Geary uses.

edges.relationship: In Trial by Fire and Water (1986) Bartlett labels Peter Brown's account of the ordeal as a consensus-building device that lapsed as coercive authority grew ‘the functionalist approach’ and rejects it, tying the ordeal's spread instead to the growth of royal power (as read by Heikki Pihlajamäki, 1997).
edges.evidence_note: Mediated through a named scholarly reader; Bartlett's book is unread. Heikki Pihlajamäki, Evidence, Crime, and the Legal Profession (Lund: Institutet för rättshistorisk forskning, Rättshistoriskt bibliotek 54, 1997), p. 33, read in the Olin Foundation's own digital edition: ‘Peter Brown departs from the idea that the medieval world at the time of ordeals was consensus-minded’, ordeals maintaining group cohesion until coercive authority made them unnecessary (n. 30: Brown 1982, p. 324, i.e. ‘Society and the Supernatural’, reprinted in Society and the Holy in Late Antiquity); ‘Bartlett calls this “the functionalist approach” and rejects it’, linking the increased use of ordeals to royal power and calling the ordeal an ‘adjunct of royal power’ (n. 31: Bartlett 1988, pp. 34–43, the paperback of the 1986 Clarendon book; n. 32: Bartlett 1988, pp. 70–102). Pihlajamäki's footnote numbering is partly garbled in the digital text, so the exact Bartlett page ranges are his and uncollated. Brown's essay (cited by Pihlajamäki as Brown 1982) and Bartlett's chapters remain unread; the claim is Pihlajamäki's account of Bartlett's argument, not a fresh reading of either original. Pihlajamäki also notes difficulties in Bartlett's own explanation of abolition; not used here.

edges.relationship: Darnton's ‘In Search of the Enlightenment’ (Journal of Modern History, 1971) was a largely critical review of Gay's The Enlightenment, judging his intellectual history old-fashioned and arguing that his dialectical scheme of a classical appeal against Christianity failed: if antiquity was so decisive, why did the Enlightenment not begin in the Renaissance? (as read by Velema 2014 and Edelstein 2012).
edges.evidence_note: Mediated through two named readers; Darnton's review (JMH 43, 1971, 113–132) is unread. (1) Wyger Velema, ‘Oude waarheden’, Tijdschrift voor Geschiedenis 127:2 (2014), p. 230 and n. 3, read in the published version in the UvA institutional repository (Dutch; paraphrase mine): Darnton's review argued that the form of intellectual history Gay practised was ‘bijzonder ouderwets’ (particularly old-fashioned) and that ‘diens hele dialectische schema niet deugde’; if the classical tradition had mattered so much, why had the Enlightenment not begun in the Renaissance; for Darnton sixteenth- and seventeenth-century thinkers ‘van Bacon tot Newton’ stood at its cradle, and Gay had smuggled them in ‘via een achterdeur’, undermining his thesis; Velema speaks of ‘het scherpe meningsverschil tussen Darnton en Gay’. (2) Dan Edelstein, ‘The Classical Turn in Enlightenment Studies’, Modern Intellectual History 9:1 (2012), 61–71, publisher's opening extract read: ‘Robert Darnton hailed this rising tide of social and cultural history in a 1971 largely critical review of Gay's two volumes’ (n. 2). Page of the Edelstein sentence not visible (opening of the article). Gay's reply, if any, was not searched. Distinct from edge_2720 (Anderson → Darnton).
edges.map_label: Social history of ideas against Gay, 1971

edges.relationship: The Enlightenment: An Interpretation (1966–69), presented as a ‘social history of ideas’, read the philosophes' appeal to antiquity, tension with Christianity and pursuit of modernity as the beginning of Western modernity, against Carl Becker's secularized-Christianity reading, and became a standard work.
edges.evidence_note: A reader's account, read. Velema (2014), pp. 229–230 (UvA repository, published version): Gay's ‘monumentale studie’, ‘door de auteur … gepresenteerd als een proeve van de “social history of ideas”’, in fact a fairly traditional history of ideas treating the Enlightenment as a unity centred on Paris; Gay presented it ‘nadrukkelijk’ as the beginning of Western modernity, opposing Carl Becker's 1932 reading (n. 2); his dialectic of ‘the appeal to antiquity’, ‘the tension with Christianity’ and ‘the pursuit of modernity’; the book ‘groeide uit tot een standaardwerk’ but closed an era rather than opening one. Velema n. 1 cites Gay's methodological essay ‘The social history of ideas: Ernst Cassirer and after’ (in The Critical Spirit, 1967), unread. Publication years agree with the Yale AHA citation already on the atlas (tc234_gay_yale). Gay's volumes are unread. Becker and Cassirer are not atlas endpoints.

edges.relationship: Gay dates his turn to Freud to c. 1950–51 at Columbia, when Franz Neumann, ‘tied to the Frankfurt School’, began a serious reading course on Freud with Herbert Marcuse taking part (Gay 1997).
edges.evidence_note: His own retrospective testimony, read. ‘The Psychoanalytically-Informed Historian’ (interview, September 1997; cliospsyche.org excerpt), answer to ‘What brought you to psychohistory?’: ‘an older colleague, Franz Neumann, who was a left-wing Marxist’; ‘Having been tied to the Frankfurt School he had some interest in Freud’; Neumann's circle ‘started this serious course of reading on Freud’, with ‘their best friend, Herbert Marcuse’; Gay calls himself an amateur then and dates professional training to the mid-1970s. The route is social and personal: it does not claim Gay adopted critical theory, and Neumann and Marcuse are not atlas endpoints, so the edge attaches to the group endpoint on Gay's own identification of Neumann with the Frankfurt School. Velema (2014) n. 1 independently records Gay's 1967 methodological essay appearing in a volume of essays in honour of Marcuse. Retrospective recollection, not contemporaneous evidence. Complements edge_2935 (Freud → Gay).

edges.relationship: Thompson recalls that by the second edition of The Voice of the Past (1988) oral historians had been strongly influenced by Luisa Passerini and ‘even more’ by Portelli's ideas that changes in memory are part of its value, which led him to add a wholly new chapter, ‘Memory and the Self’.
edges.evidence_note: His own retrospective testimony, read. Life story interview with Karen Worcman (1996, 2002), UK Data Archive thematic highlights (SN 6226, June 2017), section 15 ‘Towards subjectivity’, printed p. 13: ‘by the time of the second edition, ten years later, all the people in oral history had been very strongly influenced both by Luisa Passerini on her ideas about subjectivity and silence, and memory, and I think even more by [Portelli] and his ideas about the way in which people changed memory, and how that is part of the value of memory. So there's a whole chapter on “Memory and the Self”, which is completely new, in the second edition.’ The transcript reads ‘Sandra Portelli’, a transcription error for Sandro (Alessandro) Portelli; the identification is the researcher's. Section 14, p. 12: in 1977 the first edition was ‘very much a positivistic work’. Only professional-method passages used; the interview story Thompson tells in section 15 is not reproduced. The 1988 chapter itself is unread (the atlas's reader extract covers community history only), so the edge records Thompson's account of the debt, not a reading of how the chapter uses Portelli. Passerini is not an atlas endpoint. Refines the description's existing contrast with Passerini and Portelli into a documented route.

edges.relationship: Tosh's The Pursuit of History (1991 edition) calls What Is History? ‘still unsurpassed as a stimulating and provocative statement by a radically inclined scholar’ and makes the Carr–Elton controversy ‘the best starting-point’ for debate on the standing of historical knowledge (as quoted by Alun Munslow, 1997).
edges.evidence_note: Read 2026-10-31 through a named reader with exact locators: Alun Munslow, review of What Is History? (November 1997), History in Focus 2 (IHR), ¶2 quoting ‘still unsurpassed as a stimulating and provocative statement by a radically inclined scholar’ (Tosh 1991: 234) and ¶3 quoting ‘The controversy between Carr and Elton is the best starting-point for the debate about the standing of historical knowledge’ (Tosh 1991: 236); bibliography: ‘Tosh, John (1991) The Pursuit of History London, Longman.’ Tosh's book itself is unread here; the words are as Munslow quotes them. The claim is that Tosh's textbook takes Carr's book as a reference point and recommends it; it does not make Tosh a follower of Carr's positions (he pairs Carr with Elton). Elton has no endpoint, so the controversy itself cannot be an edge.
edges.map_label: What Is History? as Tosh's starting point, 1991

edges.relationship: Fitzpatrick names Carr as one of the two scholars in England who ‘knew something about’ her planned doctoral research and encouraged it, and recalls admiring him and his way of working (interview, 2012); Menashe (1996) counts Carr among the ‘spiritual godfathers’ of revisionism, a movement in which he singles out her work.
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read 2026-10-31. Baltic Worlds interview (BW 1, 2012, print pp. 4–10; conducted 5 January 2012; interviewer not named on the page), answer on her doctoral years: ‘The two people who knew something about what I wanted to do were E. H. Carr in Cambridge and Leonard Schapiro at the London School of Economics’; ‘I admired Carr. I found him to be a fascinating figure’; ‘I was quite fascinated by his way of working which was completely different from mine’; she adds that ‘Carr was remote’ and that, writing on politics and economics in the 1920s, ‘he had the sources’. The editorial sidebar (not her words) calls Carr ‘one of Sheila Fitzpatrick's mentors during her stay in England’. A named reader, read: Louis Menashe, ‘Revising the Revisionists’, ILWCH 50 (1996), note 1 (displayed reference note on the Cambridge page): ‘Spiritual godfathers of revisionism were Isaac Deutscher and E. H. Carr’, Carr for his ‘insistence on value-free explorations of Soviet society’; the same note says the study of popular support was ‘a project undertaken with the greatest skill by Sheila Fitzpatrick’ (citing Education and Social Mobility, 1978, and The Russian Revolution, 1982). Limits: personal admiration and early support, and one reader's genealogy of revisionism; she stresses that her method differed from his. No supervision, co-authorship or adoption of Carr's political judgements is claimed. Her memoir A Spy in the Archives (2013; MUP blurb read, no Carr mention) and the LRB essay of the same title (2010, read, no Carr mention) do not add evidence; Menashe's article body unread (no abstract; first page an image). Reviewer 2026-10-31: same answer adds ‘I spoke to those two people and both of them were very encouraging to me’ and ‘we got quite friendly, I think’.
edges.map_label: Carr and the young Fitzpatrick; revisionism's godfather

edges.relationship: Everyday Stalinism (1999) asks how Soviet city dwellers managed ordinary lives in the extraordinary conditions of the 1930s, and the joint chapter with Alf Lüdtke (2008) takes the everyday in Nazi Germany and Stalinist Russia as the ground on which to test Arendt's atomization thesis, asking whether social relationships broke down and were perhaps reconfigured.
edges.evidence_note: Read 2026-10-31. A reader of the book: J. Arch Getty, ‘Palaces on Monday’, LRB 22:5 (2 March 2000), review of Everyday Stalinism, full text: ¶1 the shift from the ‘totalitarian model’ to a ‘new Soviet social history’ that ‘insisted that society mattered, even in dictatorships’; ¶4 ‘Strictly empirical analysis is her preferred method’; ¶6 the book's question, ‘how did ordinary people manage?’; ¶9 shopping as, ‘in Fitzpatrick's phrase, a “survival skill”’. Joint chapter (Cambridge page summary, read): Fitzpatrick and Lüdtke, ‘Energizing the Everyday: On the Breaking and Making of Social Bonds in Nazism and Stalinism’, in Geyer and Fitzpatrick, eds., Beyond Totalitarianism (2008), pp. 266–301, takes ‘the everyday in Nazi Germany and Stalinist Russia’ as the place where relationships broke and were possibly reconfigured; Lüdtke is the Alltagsgeschichte figure named on the micro node. Her own caveat (Baltic Worlds 2012, read): Everyday Stalinism is ‘a very atheoretical book. There is all this theory on the everyday, and I pay little attention to it.’ So the edge records a contribution to the history of everyday life, not adherence to Alltagsgeschichte or microstoria method. The book itself is unread; the existing social and Arendt edges (edge_2916, edge_2918) already use the joint chapter for different claims. Reviewer 2026-10-31: the Cambridge summary's wording is that the authors took Arendt's atomization hypothesis as the ‘starting point for our comparative inquiry into the everyday in Nazi Germany and Stalinist Russia that in each case some kind of breakdown (but perhaps also a reconfiguration?) of social relationships took place’; ‘remade’ is not claimed.

edges.relationship: Israel argues that Pocock's ‘family of enlightenments’ in Barbarism and Religion underestimates what the national strands shared and how far they fall into radical and moderate currents, and that Pocock's ecclesiastical emphasis undermines his own case for pluralism (Journal of the History of Ideas, 2016)
edges.evidence_note: Read 2026-10-31: author abstract (Crossref-deposited, as printed) of Israel, ‘J. G. A. Pocock and the “Language of Enlightenment” in His Barbarism and Religion’, JHI 77:1 (2016): 107–127. Pocock ‘argues for a “family of enlightenments,” disputing accounts, particularly Venturi’s and Gay’s, of it as a unified phenomenon’; Israel ‘asserts, however, that Pocock’s reconfiguration of different national contexts … underestimates their commonality and the degree to which they fall into the recognizable currents of radical and moderate’; ‘Pocock’s attention to the ecclesiastical and theological dimensions of the Enlightenment undermines rather than supports his argument for its pluralism.’ Context, read: Wolin's symposium introduction abstract (JHI 77:1, 99–106) places the essay in a symposium that ends with ‘a concluding response by Pocock’, arising from a CUNY conference in 2010; John Robertson's review of Barbarism and Religion I–II (Cromohs 6, 2001) had already written that ‘Pocock's Enlightenment is directly opposed to that with which Jonathan Israel has just presented us’. Article body and Pocock's response unread (Project MUSE challenge page). The edge is Israel's critique; Pocock's reply is not represented.

edges.relationship: Israel charges that Darnton, with other social and cultural historians of the Enlightenment, ‘hardly engage[s] with ideas at all’, citing Darnton's neglect of d'Holbach's place at the top of his own lists of clandestine best-sellers (H-France Forum response, 2014)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, read 2026-10-31: Israel, response essay, H-France Forum 9:1 (Winter 2014), no. 5, on Democratic Enlightenment (2011). P. 85: ‘Darnton, Chartier, Jacob, Goodman, Roche, Lilti, and others err in my estimation not in claiming ideas are refracted, modified, used selectively, ignored, and twisted—that is all too true, but because they hardly engage with ideas at all’; ‘A striking instance … is Darnton’s treatment of d’Holbach whose books regularly topped his lists of the most widely selling clandestine texts, an astounding fact which, however, he completely ignores’ (n. 25 cites Darnton, The Corpus of Clandestine Literature in France 1769–1789, 1995, pp. 194, 199, 206, 227). P. 82: he accepts being judged ‘lacking in deference towards universally admired heroes of scholarship like Furet, Darnton, and Baker’ and seeks ‘to demonstrate the shortcomings of their ubiquitously venerated views’. Darnton is the one historian in the passage given a specific charge, so he alone is proposed. The polemic is Israel's; Darnton's books are unread here and no reply by Darnton was found. Distinct from edge_2867 (Israel ↔ Cambridge contextualism).

edges.relationship: De Dijn (2012) reads Israel's Enlightenment trilogy as reviving, ‘albeit in a dramatic new form’, the modernization thesis first formulated by Peter Gay, that the Enlightenment helped create modern liberal democracy
edges.evidence_note: A named reader, read 2026-10-31: Annelien de Dijn, ‘The Politics of Enlightenment: From Peter Gay to Jonathan Israel’, Historical Journal 55:3 (2012): 785–805, author abstract: the view that the Enlightenment played ‘a crucial role in the creation of the modern, liberal democracies of the West’ was ‘first formulated by Peter Gay’; ‘Jonathan Israel's trilogy on the Enlightenment has revived the modernization thesis, albeit in a dramatic new form’; yet even Israel's work ‘does not convincingly demonstrate’ the link. Israel himself cites this article (H-France Forum 9:1, 2014, n. 41, citing p. 799) when rejecting the claim of a consensus against him. Undirected comparison drawn by de Dijn: no personal debt from Gay to Israel is asserted, and the article body is unread. Pocock's disputing of Gay's unified Enlightenment (Israel 2016 abstract) is a separate matter for Gay's entry.

edges.relationship: In his Warwick opening (1995), Smith disputes Hobsbawm's view of the nation as largely ‘invented traditions’ and above all his denial of any connection between popular ‘proto-national’ communities and later nationalisms: ‘This is exactly where I disagree’
edges.evidence_note: Read 2026-10-31: Smith's opening, Warwick debate, 24 October 1995 (published Nations and Nationalism, 1996), LSE Gellner resource page. In the passage beginning ‘It is, of course, in the deconstructionist models of Benedict Anderson and Eric Hobsbawm’: ‘In Hobsbawm's approach, the nation is seen, in large part, as a set of “invented traditions”’ (citing Hobsbawm and Ranger 1983, ch. 1); both models aim to ‘debunk nationalist views of the nation as somehow “primordial” and “perennial”’. In the passage beginning ‘But the third problem is the most crucial’: Hobsbawm ‘goes so far as to deny any connection between the popular “Proto-national” communities’ and later political nationalisms (citing Hobsbawm 1990, ch. 2); ‘This is exactly where I disagree’; ‘Modern political nationalisms cannot be understood without reference to these earlier ethnic ties and memories.’ (The page's OCR prints ‘Erie Hobsbawm’.) Smith accepts that nations are partly planned; the critique concerns the neglect of ethnic persistence, not a denial that invention occurs. Hobsbawm's reply, if any, unread; Smith's 1991 Millennium article ‘The Nation: Invented, Imagined, Reconstructed?’ is unread (no abstract obtainable).
edges.map_label: Against invented tradition and no proto-national link, 1995

edges.relationship: Smith (Warwick opening, 1995) grants that neither Anderson nor Hobsbawm treats the nation as ‘a wholly imaginary category’, accepting Anderson's ‘imagined political community’ provided that calling the nation imagined does not ‘gainsay its reality or consider it a fabrication’, and holds against modernist accounts that nations are also products of ‘preexisting traditions and heritages’.
edges.evidence_note: Read 2026-10-31: Smith's Warwick opening (1995; published 1996), same passage as smith_rel_01: ‘In Anderson's model, the nation is seen as an “imagined political community”’, ‘imagined as both finite and sovereign’ (citing Anderson 1983, ch. 3). In the following passage (‘This seems to me quite proper’) Smith agrees on condition: the nation is not ‘a wholly imaginary category’; to call it imagined should not ‘gainsay its reality or consider it a fabrication’ (his example: the Parthenon is both imagined and real); nations are ‘products of preexisting traditions and heritages which have coalesced over the generations’. A qualified critique that grants part of Anderson's view; Anderson's own text and any reply unread here. Reviewer 2026-10-31: the passage opens with Smith's concession ‘I do not think that either would regard the nation as a wholly imaginary category’, and the proviso is addressed to Anderson and Hobsbawm together; the edge is a qualified critique of Anderson's modernism, not a charge that he treats nations as fabrications.

edges.relationship: As Leonid Grinin reads it (2026), Tilly's ‘Does Modernization Breed Revolution?’ (1973) argued against Huntington's idea of a correlation between modernization and revolution, while conceding that population growth, industrialization, urbanization and other large structural changes affect the probabilities of revolution indirectly.
edges.evidence_note: Mediated, read 2026-10-31; the 1973 original is unread. Bibliographic: Charles Tilly, ‘Does Modernization Breed Revolution?’, Comparative Politics 5:3 (April 1973): 425–447 (Crossref), reprinted in Goldstone, ed., Revolutions (1986), pp. 47–57, beside Huntington's ‘Revolution and Political Order’ (pp. 39–47). A named reader: Leonid E. Grinin, ‘Modernization as a Factor of Revolutionary Destabilization in Historical Process and in Modern Africa’, Journal of Globalization Studies 17:1 (May 2026), section 1 (‘Revolutions and Modernization Period’): ‘There exist diametrically opposed views on the character of these relations (see, e.g., Huntington-Tilly's debate [Huntington 1986; Tilly 1986])’; ‘Tilly (Ibid.: 57) finally admits that, though indirectly, population growth, industrialization, urbanization, and other large-scale structural changes do, to be sure, affect the probabilities of revolution’; n. 4 refers to Tilly ‘arguing against Huntington's idea about correlation between modernization and revolutions’. The JSTOR page did not load. Before acceptance the reviewer should read Tilly's article (JSTOR 421272) to confirm that Huntington is named and to give a page; until then the edge rests on one reader. Reviewer 2026-10-31: the article was again unreadable through an authorised route (JSTOR challenge; no repository deposit found). Grinin's ‘Huntington-Tilly's debate’ cites the two texts as reprinted in Goldstone (1986), a juxtaposition rather than a published exchange; the edge rests on Grinin's attributed reading.

edges.relationship: Giddens presents his historical sociology as A Contemporary Critique of Historical Materialism (1981; volume two, The Nation-State and Violence, 1985), arguing in a 1985 lecture that Marxist and liberal accounts of the state alike lack a satisfactory treatment of the nation-state and nationalism
edges.evidence_note: Read 2026-10-31, bounded. The book title states the relation: Giddens, A Contemporary Critique of Historical Materialism (Macmillan, 1981; Crossref book and chapter metadata, including ‘Property and Class Society’ and ‘Time, Labour and the City’); Skocpol's review in Social Forces 66:1 (1987) is catalogued under ‘The Nation-State and Violence: Volume Two of a Contemporary Critique of Historical Materialism’. Argument, abstract only: the journal abstract of the transcribed lecture ‘The Nation-State and Violence’ (Valencia, 25 September 1985; Spanish translation in Relaciones Internacionales 5, 2007) says Giddens holds that Marxist and liberal thought on the state ‘coincide when they define it as a coordinating frame in which the economic relations develop, but that both of them lack a satisfactory treatment of the nation-state and nationalism’, and proposes concepts to fill the gap. The books' bodies and the lecture text are unread (Springer pages returned 404; the journal site blocked automated access). The edge records a critique and reworking of historical materialism, not a rejection of Marx in every respect.
edges.map_label: A contemporary critique of historical materialism, 1981–85

edges.relationship: Latour describes actor-network theory as a change of metaphor from surfaces to filaments, ‘or rhyzomes in Deleuze’s parlance’, and likens a network that has no outside to ‘Deleuze’s lightning rod’ (written 1990; English 1996)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, read 2026-10-31 in the author's web version (P-67) of ‘On Actor-Network Theory: A Few Clarifications plus More than a Few Complications’ (written 1990; Danish in Philosophia 25:3–4; English in Soziale Welt 47, 1996, pp. 369–381). Web p. 3: ‘Put too simply AT is a change of methaphors to describe essences: instead of surfaces one gets filaments (or rhyzomes in Deleuze’s parlance 197-).’ Web p. 6: a network ‘is not a foreground over a background, nor a crack onto a solid soil, it is like Deleuze’s lightning rod that creates by the same stroke the background and the foreground (Deleuze, 197-)’. Spellings and the unfinished ‘197-’ references are in the draft. Two acknowledged borrowings of image and vocabulary in a programmatic text; not a claim that ANT derives from Deleuze, and printed Soziale Welt pages are not collated. Latour's 1997 Keele talk ‘On Recalling ANT’ (Lancaster web version, read) attributes the label ‘actant-rhyzome ontology’ to Mike Lynch and does not mention Deleuze, so it is not cited for this edge.
